concepts.title: Meaning of Organising
concepts.definition: The managerial process that puts plans into motion by spelling out jobs and working relationships and by deploying people and resources so that the intended results are actually achieved.
concepts.key_idea: It coordinates human effort, gathers resources and welds the two into one working whole for the stated objectives.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 150-187 (Meaning; school fete example; definitions by Louis Allen and Theo Haimann)
question_patterns: what is meant by organising as a function of management
define organising and explain how it initiates implementation of plans
how does organising coordinate human efforts and resources
why is organising called a means to turn plans into action
explain organising with the example of arranging a school event

solution_steps.explain: Organising coordinates efforts, assembles resources and integrates them into a unified whole for the stated goals.
Plans stay on paper until jobs, relationships and resources are arranged -- that arrangement is organising.
A school fete run through food, decoration and ticketing committees under one coordinator shows the function at work.

concepts.title: Steps in the Process of Organising
concepts.definition: Four ordered steps: split the total work into manageable activities, group similar activities into departments, hand each post its duties matched to the person's competence, and settle who reports to whom by fixing authority relationships.
concepts.key_idea: Departmentalisation can rest on territory or product; the last step builds the hierarchy that later channels coordination.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 188-309 (Steps i to iv: division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties, reporting relationships)
question_patterns: what are the steps in the process of organising
explain departmentalisation as a step of organising
why must duties be assigned according to the ability of employees
what happens after the work is divided into manageable activities
why is establishing reporting relationships the last step of organising

solution_steps.action: List the four steps in order
solution_steps.explain: Identification and division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties, establishing authority and reporting relationships.

solution_steps.action: Explain each step in a line
solution_steps.explain: Divide to avoid duplication, group similar work for specialisation, match jobs to skills, then settle reporting lines.
Together the steps create a hierarchical structure that enables coordination among departments.

concepts.title: Importance of Organising
concepts.definition: The payoffs of doing the function well: routine tasks build worker specialisation, reporting lines become unambiguous, resources stop being duplicated, the structure can bend with the environment, administration runs clearly, people grow through delegation, and the firm gains room to expand and diversify.
concepts.key_idea: Seven benefits -- specialisation, clarity in working relationships, optimum resource use, adaptation to change, effective administration, development of personnel, expansion and growth.
question_patterns: explain the importance of organising for a business enterprise
how does organising lead to benefits of specialisation
which benefit of organising helps a firm adjust to a changing environment
how does organising help in the development of personnel
organising facilitates expansion and growth justify
how does organising bring clarity in working relationships

solution_steps.explain: Recall the seven standard benefits of organising.
For instance, delegation inside a sound structure frees managers for growth work while training subordinates.
Well-organised firms absorb environmental change and keep growing; badly organised ones stall.

concepts.title: Organisation Structure and Span of Management
concepts.definition: The frame inside which a firm's managerial and operating tasks are carried out, mapping the relationships among people, work and resources; the span of management -- how many subordinates one superior can effectively supervise -- decides how many levels the structure will carry.
concepts.key_idea: As firms grow, coordination needs a reviewed structure; a wrong structure, Drucker warns, can wreck performance.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 476-584 (Organisation Structure; span of management; travel agency example)
question_patterns: what is meant by organisation structure
define span of management and state its effect on the structure
why does a growing enterprise need to review its organisation structure
how does an organisation chart show authority and responsibility
what does the framework of an organisation specify

solution_steps.explain: It is the framework for managerial and operating tasks, specifying relationships between people, work and resources.
Span of management is the number of subordinates a superior can effectively manage; it fixes the number of levels.
With size and new functions, coordination suffers unless the structure is redesigned -- as the travel agency division into operations, sales and administration shows.

concepts.title: Functional Structure
concepts.definition: A design that groups jobs of a similar nature into separate departments such as production, purchase, marketing, accounts and personnel, all reporting to one coordinating head.
concepts.key_idea: Strengths: specialisation, easy training, minimal duplication and economies of scale. Weaknesses: functional empires, inter-department conflict and narrow outlook; it suits large firms needing deep specialisation.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 595-722 (Functional structure, advantages a-f, disadvantages a-d, suitability)
question_patterns: what is a functional structure of organisation
state any two circumstances under which the functional structure is appropriate
explain the advantages of a functional structure
what are the disadvantages of grouping jobs by functions
why does a functional structure make training of employees easier
how can a functional structure create functional empires

solution_steps.explain: Similar and related jobs are grouped under one major function, each function becoming a department.
Specialisation, control within departments, efficiency, low duplication, simpler training, attention to every function.
Departmental interest can trump organisational interest; coordination across functions is hard. It fits large, specialised operations.

concepts.title: Divisional Structure
concepts.definition: A design built from separate self-contained business units, one per product line or market, each headed by a divisional manager who owns the unit's performance and runs its own production, marketing and finance functions as a profit centre.
concepts.key_idea: Merits: product specialisation, accountability for profits, faster decisions, easy expansion. Demerits: inter-division conflict over funds, costly duplication of functions, powerful heads; it suits multi-product enterprises.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 723-902 (Divisional structure, advantages a-d, disadvantages a-c, suitability, comparison table)
question_patterns: what is a divisional structure of organisation
why is each division called a profit centre
a cosmetics firm adds a footwear and a garments line which structure suits it
compare the functional and divisional structures on cost and coordination
how does a divisional structure help in fixing responsibility for performance
state the disadvantages of a divisional structure

solution_steps.explain: Separate divisions are formed for each product line, each multifunctional and self-contained.
Divisional heads grow versatile, profits are traceable to each unit, decisions come fast, new divisions slot in without disturbing the rest.
Divisions may fight over funds and duplicate functions at extra cost; the design fits firms with many varied products.

concepts.title: Formal Organisation
concepts.definition: The deliberately designed structure of authority and responsibility that management creates to get its plans carried out, with clear boundaries of who reports to whom and rules that guide conduct.
concepts.key_idea: It puts work above personal ties, keeps unity of command and stability, but can breed procedural delays and stiffle creativity; its structure may be functional or divisional.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 1078-1238 (Formal organisation: meaning, features a-e, advantages, limitations)
question_patterns: what is meant by formal organisation
state the features of a formal organisation
explain the advantages and limitations of formal organisation
why can a formal organisation lead to procedural delays
who designs the formal structure and for what purpose
how does the formal organisation maintain unity of command

solution_steps.explain: It is the management-designed structure specifying authority, responsibility and reporting lines for achieving set objectives.
Defined interrelationships among positions, a means to plan achievement, coordination of departments, deliberate design, work over personalities.
Fixable responsibility, no role ambiguity, stability -- against procedural delay and little room for creative deviation.

concepts.title: Informal Organisation
concepts.definition: The web of personal and social relationships that springs up by itself when colleagues interact beyond their official roles -- lunch groups, cricket circles, gossip networks -- with no written rules and no fixed direction of communication.
concepts.key_idea: It arises from within the formal structure, obeys group norms rather than rules, and can speed information and satisfy social needs -- or spread rumours and resist change; management is advised to work with it, not against it.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 1239-1423 (Informal organisation: meaning, features a-e, comparison, advantages, disadvantages)
question_patterns: what is meant by informal organisation
identify the network of social relationships arising spontaneously due to interaction at work
how does the informal organisation support the formal organisation
state the features of informal organisation
what are the disadvantages of informal organisation for management
compare formal and informal organisations on the basis of origin and communication

solution_steps.explain: Informal organisation is the spontaneous network of interpersonal relations formed out of workplace interaction.
Origin from social interaction rather than rules; authority from personal qualities; communication flows any which way.
Fast feedback, belongingness, filling formal gaps -- against rumour, resistance to change and pressure to conform.

concepts.title: Delegation and Its Three Elements
concepts.definition: The downward handover of authority by a superior to his subordinate, resting on three elements: authority, the right to command and decide; responsibility, the duty to perform the assigned task; and accountability, answerability for the final outcome, which can never be passed on.
concepts.key_idea: Authority is delegated, responsibility is assumed, accountability is imposed -- authority flows down, responsibility and accountability flow up; delegation is never abdication.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 1424-1639 (Delegation; elements: authority, responsibility, accountability; overview table)
question_patterns: what is meant by delegation of authority
discuss the elements of delegation
which element of delegation can never be delegated and why
distinguish between authority responsibility and accountability on the basis of flow
why is delegation not the same as abdication
what happens when authority granted is not commensurate with responsibility

solution_steps.explain: It is the downward transfer of authority from superior to subordinate so the manager is free for higher-priority work.
Authority: the right to act and command, flowing downward. Responsibility: the obligation to perform, flowing upward. Accountability: answerability for the result, also upward and non-transferable.
Authority must match responsibility -- surplus authority invites misuse, surplus responsibility renders a person ineffective.
Authority is delegated, responsibility is assumed, accountability is imposed or created.

concepts.title: Importance of Delegation
concepts.definition: Why handing authority down pays: managers escape routine work and manage better, subordinates grow into future leaders, employees feel trusted and motivated, expansion gets a ready cadre, the hierarchy itself stands on delegated authority, and duties stop overlapping.
concepts.key_idea: Six benefits -- effective management, employee development, motivation, facilitation of growth, basis of management hierarchy, better coordination.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 1640-1743 (Importance of Delegation i to vi)
question_patterns: why is delegation considered essential for effective organising
how does delegation develop employees for higher positions
explain the importance of delegation for a manager
how does delegation motivate employees
in what way does delegation form the basis of the management hierarchy

solution_steps.explain: Recall the six standard benefits of delegation.
Entrusting a task signals trust, builds the subordinate's self-esteem and frees the manager's time.
Delegation underpins coordination and growth, so it is a key element of effective organising.

concepts.title: Decentralisation and Its Importance
concepts.definition: The systematic spread of decision-making authority to every level of the organisation, placing decisions nearest the action; it treats dispersal of authority as a philosophy of trust in people's competence rather than a mere handover of tasks.
concepts.key_idea: Six benefits -- initiative among subordinates, managerial talent for the future, quicker decisions, relief to top management, facilitation of growth, better control; applied without balance it risks disintegration.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 1744-2042 (Decentralisation; centralisation and decentralisation as relative terms; importance i to vi)
question_patterns: what is meant by decentralisation
why would an organisation choose to decentralise explain the importance
how does decentralisation develop managerial talent for the future
decentralisation helps in quick decision making justify
how does decentralisation give relief to top management
can an organisation be completely centralised or decentralised give your view

solution_steps.explain: Decentralisation is delegation of authority spread through all levels, so decision points sit closest to operations.
Complete centralisation or complete decentralisation is unrealistic; every firm mixes the two, drifting toward decentralisation as it grows.
Initiative, managerial talent, speed of decisions, top-management relief, growth and better control -- with caution against disintegration.

concepts.title: Delegation versus Decentralisation
concepts.definition: Delegation is the compulsory, day-to-day act of a superior passing authority to an immediate subordinate to lighten his own burden, while decentralisation is an optional top-management policy that extends delegation to the lowest levels to widen subordinates' autonomy.
concepts.key_idea: Compare on five bases -- nature (compulsory act versus optional policy), freedom of action, status (process versus result of policy), scope (narrow, two persons versus organisation-wide), purpose (relief of the manager versus enlarged role of subordinates).
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs105.txt lines 2070-2123 (Delegation and Decentralisation comparative view)
question_patterns: distinguish between delegation and decentralisation
decentralisation is extending delegation to the lowest levels comment
why is delegation compulsory while decentralisation is optional
compare delegation and decentralisation on the basis of scope and purpose
which of the two is a policy decision of the top management

solution_steps.explain: Nature, freedom of action, status, scope and purpose.

Delegation: compulsory act, more control, a process, narrow scope, aims at lessening the manager's burden. Decentralisation: optional policy, greater freedom, the outcome of policy, widest scope, aims at enlarging the subordinate's role.
Decentralisation is delegation carried through the whole organisation -- the former rests on the latter.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A shoe maker plans to diversify into leather bags and western formal wear to serve working women as one-stop provider. Which structure would you recommend for the expanded firm and why?

solution_template.explain: Several distinct product lines point to a divisional structure.
Each product can become a self-contained division with its own functions, so responsibility for profits is fixed and new lines can be added freely.
Product specialisation, flexibility, fast decisions and easy expansion of the product range.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebs105.txt lines 2223-2227 (production manager and foreman exercise)
worked_examples.question_pattern: A production manager sets a 200-unit daily target for the foreman but gives him no authority to requisition tools and materials. Can the manager blame the foreman for missing the target?

solution_template.explain: Responsibility without matching authority renders a person ineffective.
The foreman holds the duty to deliver 200 units but lacks the authority to draw tools and materials, so the pairing is broken.
No -- the manager cannot fairly blame the foreman, because authority granted was not commensurate with the responsibility assigned.

worked_examples.question_pattern: An old sewing machines firm run wholly on formal lines suffers slow decisions, red tape for grievances and high turnover. What change should it bring and what will it gain?

solution_template.explain: Total dependence on formal channels brings procedural delay and suppresses voice -- the formal structure's known limitations.
Encourage the informal organisation alongside the formal one, and loosen the structure for faster flow.
Quicker feedback, satisfaction of social needs, fewer grievances bottled in red tape, lower turnover and better adaptation.
